Getting Started with ultragsea

BigOmics Analytics

Source: vignettes/ultragsea.Rmd
ultragsea.Rmd

Introduction

ultragsea is a novel, ultrafast and memory optimized gene set enrichment scoring algorithm not unlike fGSEA. ultragsea demonstrates highly correlated gene set scores and p-values and typically is 100 times faster than fGSEA.

Example

Preparing gensets

For this vignette, we retrieve the Hallmark gene sets using the msigdbr package. Of course you can use your own gene sets or download from somewhere else.

library(ultragsea)
library(msigdbr)
gs <- msigdbr::msigdbr(collection = "H")
#> Downloading gene sets (first use only, may take a few minutes)...
gmt <- tapply(gs$gene_symbol,gs$gs_name,list)
length(gmt)
#> [1] 50

Performing the statistical test

Just for this example we use some random values for fc but in general this is a fold change from some statistical comparison of your experiment.

G <- gmt2mat(gmt)
fc <- rnorm(nrow(G))
names(fc) <- rownames(G)
res <- ultragsea(G, fc, format='as.gsea', method='cor')
res <- ultragsea(G, fc, format='as.gsea', method='ztest')
head(res)
#>                               pathway       pval      padj log2err          ES
#>                                <char>      <num>     <num>   <num>       <num>
#> 1:           HALLMARK_HEME_METABOLISM 0.96527162 0.9652716      NA  0.01423022
#> 2:     HALLMARK_INFLAMMATORY_RESPONSE 0.68056175 0.8725151      NA  0.13455730
#> 3:         HALLMARK_KRAS_SIGNALING_UP 0.63095925 0.8725151      NA  0.15700453
#> 4: HALLMARK_OXIDATIVE_PHOSPHORYLATION 0.67483574 0.8725151      NA -0.13711441
#> 5:              HALLMARK_ADIPOGENESIS 0.13486035 0.6686212      NA  0.48868756
#> 6:       HALLMARK_ALLOGRAFT_REJECTION 0.07052317 0.6686212      NA -0.59109455
#>           NES  size                                 leadingEdge
#>         <num> <int>                                      <list>
#> 1:  0.0384407   200    CA2,BNIP3L,CDC27,H1-0,BCAM,BLVRA,...[33]
#> 2:  0.3634855   200    IL4R,CCL2,HBEGF,INHBA,ITGB3,EREG,...[36]
#> 3:  0.4241232   200      CA2,HBEGF,INHBA,KLF4,EREG,AKT2,...[36]
#> 4: -0.3703931   200 ACAA1,SDHC,ECHS1,GPI,GRPEL1,ATP6V1F,...[27]
#> 5:  1.3201130   200  ALDOA,ECH1,GPX4,CRAT,DHCR7,GADD45A,...[41]
#> 6: -1.5967495   200    CCND2,TIMP1,LIF,IFNGR2,CCL7,LCP2,...[41]

For the fastest speed, especially when computing enrichment for multiple foldchanges, it is better to call the low-level functions for geneset correlation or geneset z-test directly. They do not return the nicely formatted output tables as ultragsea() but they are much faster as they are optimized for matrix inputs F.

F <- cbind(fc,fc,fc,fc,fc)
res1 <- gset.cortest(G, F, compute.p=TRUE)
res2 <- gset.ztest(G, F)

Plotting

You can proceed by plotting the gene set using e.g. the plotting functions of the fgsea package.

#library(fgsea)
#k <- res$pathway[which.min(res$pval)]
#fgsea::plotEnrichment(gmt[[k]],fc,ticksSize = 0.2)
